newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q1 GDP, foreign debt data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian Q1 GDP, foreign debt data.

text.p: The average measure of Australian gross domestic product (GDP-A) grew by 0.9 percent in the March quarter, the Bureau of Statistics reported on Wednesday.
In annual terms, GDP rose by 2.4 percent.
This compared with median market forecasts of a rise of 0.8 percent for the quarter and a 2.2 percent annual rate.
The Bureau also said March quarter foreign debt came in at A$199.902 billion compared with median forecasts of A$204.7 billion.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
CRAIG JAMES, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The figures were broadly in line with market expectations. But taking December and March together, growth remains reasonably modest. There is no signs of price pressure. The Australian economy can afford to grow more quickly. And as such an easing of monetary policy is still likely."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"I don't think (the GDP figure) has any particular implications for monetary policy and the focus now will shift to whether the apparent pick-up in growth in the March quarter, compared with the 0.4 percent for the December quarter, carried through into the June quarter or not ... It dampens (expectations of another official interest rate cut) a bit. It does not eliminate it all together, but this figure never was going to do that. It's really second-quarter data that's the key to that question."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"It's pretty much neutral for the market. We've seen the bill futures sell off marginally. There has been some speculation of rate cut ... The numbers today are really in line with what we had been expecting so there is nothing really for the bulls at the short-end, but there is certainly nothing to put away bullish expectations either. The good news is on the deflator, coming up 0.3 percent. That's about 1.5 percent on the year, and very much in line with numbers the Reserve Bank would be wanting to see, and it's certainly is quite a good inflation indicator. The economy was going reasonable well in the March quarter, but the question is will it continue into June."
CHRIS RICHARDSON, DIRECTOR, ACCESS ECONOMICS:

"The real story is in domestic demand, which troughed last September quarter and is now rising at its fastest quarterly rate for 2-1/2 years. The only thing standing between this and a robust March GDP figure was the rundown in stocks. The rundown was sufficiently violent to suggest that at least a proportion of it was unintended. So from here on, growth will look better."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"They were pretty much on track. The slowdown in the economy has come through quite evidently. The composition of growth is quite interesting in that growth is now at its lowest point for a few years ... The Reserve Bank and the Treasury are talking about 4.0 percent growth in the second half of the year, and given that we have finally seen the inventories starting to be run down, the pre-conditions are there for a pick-up in growth as we get through the remainder of 1997."
ANTHONY THOMPSON, DOMESTIC ECONOMIST, HONG KONG BANK:

"Focusing mainly on GDP, I think it is a real no surprises set of numbers. It's good that the quarterly growth rate was slightly higher than expected and that the annual rate, because of revisions, was higher than expected as well. I think this is going to represent the low point in the economic cycle with annual growth at 2.4 percent. I think the key is that indicators, subsequent to the end of the first quarter have been picking up. Aside from the latest numbers that we've had on retail trade, I think you've got to look at the positive signs that we've had in the second quarter for the housing sector."
RICHARD YETSINGA, ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:
"It was consistent with expectations basically. Inflation was well behaved. Given it was consistent with expectations (there are no policy implications)."
DAVID LANSLEY, TREASURY ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"It's not a bad result. Without the strong contribution from the public sector we would have seen a substantially softer economy. It's not all that differrent from what we're finding in the National's Bank's survey, which is of a flat private economy. You've got a mixed economy which is consistent with being at the bottom of the cycle. The Reserve Bank's not going to put a lot of weight on this as they've said often enough they're forward looking. We don't see things getting soft enough to justify another easing and we still think they'll have to tighten by the end of calendar 1997."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
